en: The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Perfect Enlightenment, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhatoṭara of Kasmīra during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān entered the Great Radiance of Supernatural Powers.
The treasury, the samādhi of right reception, the majestic abiding maintained by the light of all Tathāgatas, is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings;
it is the limit of reality where body and mind are quiescent and equal, perfectly fulfilling the ten directions in non-dual accordance, manifesting all pure lands within the realm of non-duality.

He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, whose names were Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva, Vaśitāprāpta Bodhisattva, Ghoṣavati Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva, Samantabodhi Bodhisattva, Pariniṣpannabodhi Bodhisattva, Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva, and others who served as their leaders;
together with all these retinues, they had entered into samādhi and dwelt together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the Dharma of equality.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

I pray that you will, for the sake of all the assembled Dharma-folk who have come to this gathering, explain the Tathāgata’s original practices on the ground of purity, as well as how a Bodhisattva, within the Mahāyāna, gives rise to a pure mind and remains far removed from all afflictions, so that sentient beings of future末代 (final) ages who seek the Mahāyāna shall not fall into false views.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, making this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
At that moment, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent!
Excellent!
Sons of good family,

it is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practices for attaining the ground of enlightenment for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and so that all sentient beings of the final age who seek the Mahāyāna may attain correct upholding and not fall into false views.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

“Good son! The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the *pāramitās*, as well as the instructions for training bodhisattvas.”

When all Tathāgatas first established their stage of practice, they all relied upon the aspect of perfect, illuminating, pure awakening; only by forever severing ignorance did they achieve the Buddha-way.
What is this ignorance?
Good son!

All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions, like a person who has lost their way and confuses the four directions. They falsely take the four great elements to be the characteristics of their own bodies, and the reflected shadows of the six sense objects to be the characteristics of their own minds;
they are like those with diseased eyes who see flowers in the sky or a second moon.
"Good son! In emptiness there are truly no flowers; it is the sick person who grasps at them falsely.

Because of this false grasping, one is not only deluded regarding the intrinsic nature of this empty space, but is also confused about the actual place where flowers grow. Due to this, one falsely undergoes the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance."
Good son! This ignorance has no real substance. It is like a person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing can be found.
It is also like various empty flowers vanishing into space; one cannot say there is a specific place where they are extinguished. Why is this?
Because there is no place of birth.
Within this non-arising, all sentient beings delusively perceive arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called the cycle of birth and death. Good son!

When a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, he knows these are like flowers in the sky; thus there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death. This is not because they are absent through effort, but because they are non-existent by their very nature.
That which perceives is like space; that which perceives space is like the appearance of flowers in the sky. Yet, one cannot say that the nature of perception is non-existent.
When both existence and non-existence are discarded, this is called "conformity with pure awakening."

Why is this? Because it is the nature of empty space, because it is eternally unmoving, because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing, and because there is neither cognition nor vision; and because, like the nature of the Dharmadhātu, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions.
This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the stage of the cause.
"By means of this, Bodhisattvas give rise to a pure mind within the Mahāyāna; sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this shall not fall into false views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Mañjuśrī, you should know: All Tathāgatas..."
From the ground of the original stage, one awakens through wisdom and thoroughly understands ignorance;
thus one can escape the cycle of transmigration, just like a person within a dream.
Upon awakening, nothing can be apprehended;
in this state of equanimity and immutability, awareness pervades the ten directions,
and one immediately attains the Way of the Buddha.
When all illusions have ceased, there is no place; even the attainment of the Way is non-existent, for the fundamental nature is originally perfect.
Within this, the Bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta;
may all sentient beings of the final age cultivate this to escape false views.

Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!

I pray that for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered here, and for all sentient beings of the future age who practice the Mahāyāna, you will explain how they should cultivate their practice upon hearing of this pure realm of perfect enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!
If those sentient beings know that they are like illusions, then their bodies and minds are also illusions. How can one use illusion to cultivate illusion?
If the nature of all illusions were entirely extinguished, then there would be no mind; who then would perform cultivation?”
Why, then, do you further speak of practicing according to the nature of illusion?

If all sentient beings fundamentally do not practice, but instead constantly dwell within birth and death as mere illusions, and have never understood the illusory nature of their own realm, how can they liberate their deluded minds from false conceptualization?
"I pray that for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, you will provide some skillful means for their gradual cultivation, so that these beings may forever be free from all illusions.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good sons!

You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to cultivate the bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi through skillful means and gradual stages, so as to enable all sentient beings to become free from all illusions."
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

“Good son! The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky appear from space; though the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed.
The illusory minds of sentient beings likewise depend upon illusion for their cessation; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving.”

To speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion; if one speaks of the existence of awakening, one has not yet departed from illusion, and the same applies to speaking of the non-existence of awakening.
Therefore, the extinction of illusion is called immovability.

"Good son! All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms. Because they maintain a mind that resolutely clings to such detachment, even the mind that perceives things as illusory must itself be detached. Detachment, being itself an illusion, must also be detached from; even the detachment from the detachment from illusion must be detached from. When one attains a state where there is nothing further to be detached from, all illusions are eliminated."
It is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood are used as causes for one another, fire emerges, the wood is exhausted, and the ashes fly away while the smoke vanishes.
Cultivating illusion with illusion is likewise so: although all illusions are exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation.
"Good son! To know illusion is itself to leave it; no expedient means are required.
To leave illusion is itself awakening; there is likewise no gradual succession."
"All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who practice in reliance upon this shall thus be able to forever leave all illusions behind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Samantabhadra, you should know: All sentient beings..."
The illusory ignorance that has no beginning Arises entirely from the Tathāgatas’ mind of perfect enlightenment.
Like forms appearing based on space, If these flowers in the sky were to be extinguished,
Space is fundamentally unmoving;
illusions arise from various perceptions. When illusions cease, awareness is perfected, for the mind of awareness is unmoving.
If those bodhisattvas, as well as sentient beings of the final age, [should understand this...]
One should always remain far removed from illusions, leaving behind all illusions entirely.
Just as fire arises within wood and the fire is extinguished once the wood is exhausted, so too is awakening—there is no gradual progression; the skillful means are likewise thus.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!

I pray that you will, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered here and for all sentient beings of the future age, expound the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s cultivation: how should they contemplate?
How does one maintain and sustain [the Dharma]?
For those sentient beings who have not yet attained awakening, what skillful means should be employed to cause them all to awaken?
World-Honored One!

If those sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct contemplation, they will become confused and distressed upon hearing this samādhi spoken by the Buddha-Tathāgata, and thus they will be unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment.
"We pray that you will arouse compassion and, for our sake and for the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age, provisionally explain the skillful means.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good sons!

You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of practice, contemplation, and maintenance, as well as the various provisional skillful means; therefore, listen attentively now!"
"I shall now explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.
"Good son!..."

Those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect *bodhicitta* of awakening should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, they should strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts, dwell peacefully among their followers, and sit in quietude within a still chamber, constantly reflecting thus:

"This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements. That which is called hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities all return to earth; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, froth, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the large and small excretions all return to water; warmth returns to fire; and movement returns to wind."
"When the four great elements each depart, where then would this deluded body be?
One immediately realizes that this body has no ultimate substance; it exists as a phenomenon through combination, truly identical to a magical illusion."
Through the provisional conjunction of the four conditions, the six sense organs falsely arise;

when the six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally, the energy of conditions falsely arises, which accumulates therein and appears as if it had the characteristics of conditions—this is provisionally named "mind."

Good son! This deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense objects. When the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no sense objects can be found; within them, the conditions for sense objects each return to their dissolution and extinction, such that ultimately no perceiving mind can be seen.

“Good son! Because the illusory body of those sentient beings ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease; because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion also ceases; and because the cessation of illusion ceases, that which is not illusory does not cease.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the brightness appears.”
"Good son!
You should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are forever extinguished, the ten directions will be pure.
Good son!"
For example, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects five colors, each appearing according to its direction; those who are ignorant perceive that the maṇi actually possesses these five colors.
"Good son!

The pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind. Those who are deluded claim that pure, perfect enlightenment truly exists in such a way, and they likewise maintain that the specific characteristics of body and mind exist in that same manner;
because of this, they are unable to distance themselves from illusion and transformation."
Therefore, I speak of the illusory defilements of body and mind; in contrast to those who have abandoned such illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva.
When defilements are exhausted and opposition is eliminated, there is neither the defilement to be opposed nor the one who speaks the name.

“Good son! Because this bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all illusions are but the extinction of reflected images, they then attain a purity that is directionless, manifested by the awakening to boundless empty space.

Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure; because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure; because seeing is pure, the faculty of the eye is pure; because the faculty is pure, the consciousness of the eye is pure; because that consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure; because hearing is pure, the faculty of the ear is pure; because the faculty is pure, the consciousness of the ear is pure;
because that consciousness is pure, the objects of cognition are pure. Thus it is likewise for the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Good son!

Because the sense organs are pure, the objects of form are pure; because form is pure, the objects of sound are pure; and it is likewise for the objects of fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena."
"Good son!
Because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure; and the fire and wind elements are likewise so."
"Good son!
Because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence are pure.

Because those are pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unimpeded knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure; likewise, even up to the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors, all are pure."
"Good son!

Because the nature of all true marks is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure; because many bodies are pure, and so on, even unto the perfect enlightenment of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions is pure."
"Good son!

Because one world is pure, many worlds are pure; because many worlds are pure, it extends in this way until it reaches the end of space, wherein all things throughout the three periods of time are perfectly encompassed, equal, pure, and immovable."
“Good son! Just as space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable;
because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.”
In this way, up to the eighty-four thousand dharanī-gates being equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable. Good son!
The nature of awakening is all-pervasive, pure, and immovable.
Because it is perfectly boundless, one should know that the six faculties pervade the dharma-realm;
because the faculties are all-pervasive, one should know that the six objects pervade the dharma-realm.
Because dust pervades everywhere, you should know that the four great elements pervade the dharma-realm;
in this way, even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, they pervade the dharma-realm. Good son!
Because that wondrous nature of awakening is all-pervasive, the nature of the sense organs and the nature of the sense objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled;
because the sense organs and sense objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled, it is likewise so even unto the gates of *dhāraṇī*, which are neither destroyed nor intermingled.
It is like the light of hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room: the light pervades everywhere, being neither destroyed nor intermingled.
"Good son!

Because awakening is perfected, you should know that a bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas; they do not loathe birth-and-death, nor do they crave nirvana; they do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor do they despise those who violate them; they do not value long-standing practice, nor do they slight beginners."
Why is this? Because it is the awakening of all things.
It is like the light of the eyes clearly perceiving objects before one; that light is perfect and complete, such that it is free from both aversion and attachment. Why is this?
The luminous body is non-dual, for it is free from both aversion and attachment. "Good son!
For this Bodhisattva and for sentient beings of the final age who practice this mind and achieve its realization, there is neither cultivation nor achievement."

Perfect Enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and non-dual. Within it, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sand world-systems arise and perish like scattered flowers in the sky—neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor liberated.
Only then does one know that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the beginning, and that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday.
"Good son!

Because it is like a dream from yesterday, you should know that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going. That which is realized is without gain and without loss, without grasping and without relinquishing. That which is capable of realizing is without action, without stopping, without effort, and without extinction. Within this realization, there is no subject and no object; ultimately there is neither realization nor a realizer. The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible."
Good son!

Those bodhisattvas practice in this way, proceed through these successive stages, contemplate in this way, maintain themselves in this way, employ such skillful means, and attain awakening in this way; seeking the Dharma in this manner, they do not become confused or distressed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Universal Eye, you should know: All sentient beings, in body and mind, are like illusions.
The physical form belongs to the four great elements.”
The nature of the mind returns to the six sense objects;
the four great elements are each separate in essence—what is it that brings them together?
By practicing in this manner step by step, all things become entirely pure.
Immovable and pervading the Dharma-realm, without effort, cessation, spontaneity, or extinction, there is likewise no one who can realize it.
All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky;
the three periods of time are entirely equal, ultimately without coming or going.
"Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, as well as sentient beings of the final age,
who wish to seek entry into the Buddha-way, should practice in this manner. Thereupon,

Vajragarbha Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

You have skillfully proclaimed for all the bodhisattvas the Tathāgata’s pure Great Dharani of Perfect Enlightenment—the gradual expedient means of the dharma-practice on the causal ground—to open up the ignorance of all sentient beings.
The assembly of dharma-followers here present, having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, find their illusory cataracts cleared away and their eyes of wisdom purified.”
World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all ignorance?
If all ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been enlightened from the very beginning?
Ordinary beings throughout the ten directions have fundamentally attained the Buddha-way, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance;
when, then, could any Tathāgata ever again give rise to any afflictions?

We only pray that you will not abandon your unobstructed great compassion, but open the secret treasury for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, so that they may hear such a Sūtra teaching of definitive meaning and forever sever doubt and regret.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
“Excellent!”
Excellent! Sons of good family, it is well that you are able,

for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this profound, secret, and ultimate skillful means— the most supreme instruction of the bodhisattvas and the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna— which can cause all bodhisattvas practicing and studying in the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings of the final age, to attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

“Good son! The beginning and end, birth and death, prior and subsequent, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, arising and ceasing of all worlds—these continuous successions of thought-moments, their cyclic recurrence, and their various acts of grasping and rejecting, are all saṃsāra.”
If one attempts to discern perfect enlightenment while still remaining within saṃsāra, that nature of perfect enlightenment will itself be subject to the cycle of transmigration;
there is no possibility of escaping saṃsāra in such a state.
It is like trying to stir a tranquil pool of water by moving one's eyes.
Furthermore, it is like a firebrand whirled by a steady eye;
it is also like this when clouds move and the moon appears to travel, or when a boat moves and the shore seems to shift. Good son!
If those rotations have not yet ceased, it is impossible to find that object abiding beforehand;

how much more so for one whose mind is defiled by the cycle of birth and death and has never been purified—how could such a person contemplate the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment without being drawn back into the cycle?
For this reason, you have given rise to three delusions. "Good sons!
It is like illusory cataracts that falsely perceive flowers in the sky; if the illusory cataracts are removed, one cannot say: "
"Now that this cataract has been extinguished, when will all other cataracts ever arise again?
Why is this? Because the two phenomena—the cataract and the flower—are not mutually dependent.
It is also like the case of flowers in the sky: when they vanish into the sky, one cannot say that the sky will ever again give rise to flowers.
Why? Because the sky originally has no flowers, as it is subject neither to arising nor to ceasing.
Birth-and-death and nirvana are identical in their arising and ceasing; the wondrous enlightenment of perfect illumination is free from the cataracts of delusion.

Good son, you should know that space is neither temporarily existent nor temporarily non-existent; how much more so is the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment, which accords with reality and is the equal, fundamental nature of space?
“Good son! It is like refining gold ore: the gold does not come into existence through the refining;
once it has become gold, it cannot be turned back into ore again, and even after an infinite amount of time, the nature of the gold remains indestructible.”
One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished; the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is likewise so.

Good son! Within the wondrous, perfect, enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no bodhi nor nirvana; there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood; there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor the absence of saṃsāra.

“Good son! The sphere of realization of the śrāvakas—in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished—can ultimately never reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own direct realization; how much less could they fathom the Tathāgata’s sphere of perfect enlightenment with a mind of discursive thought?
It is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow; it can never ignite it.
Likewise, one who generates a mind of saṃsāra and gives rise to views of saṃsāra can never reach the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction.
Therefore, I say that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra. Good son!

Any conceptualization involving volitional effort arises from the mind; it is entirely the breath-like energy of deluded thoughts conditioned by the six sense objects, not the true essence of the mind, being like flowers in the sky.

To use such contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha is like a flower in the sky further producing fruit in the sky; it is a case of successive delusive imaginings, and no such thing can exist. Good son!
"With a false and frivolous mind full of clever views, you will be unable to accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.
Such discrimination is not a correct question.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Vajragarbha, you should know that the Tathāgata’s nature of quiescence has never had beginning or end. Through conceptual thought,
it merely revolves back again, reaching only as far as the limits of saṃsāra."
They cannot enter the ocean of the Buddha.
Gold does not exist because it has been melted; though it was originally gold, it is ultimately realized through the process of melting.
Once it has become the substance of pure gold, [it remains so].
They will never again become ore.
Birth-and-death and nirvana, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are equally the appearance of flowers in the sky.
Even contemplation is like a magical illusion; how much more so the pursuit of what is false?
"If one can thoroughly understand this mind, only then may one seek Perfect Enlightenment.

Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!"

He extensively reveals the secret treasury for the sake of the bodhisattvas, causing the great assembly to deeply awaken to saṃsāra and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. He is able to bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way, so that they may give rise to resolute faith in Great Nirvāṇa and no longer follow the realms of cyclic existence to give rise to views of transmigration.
World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, how should they sever the root of saṃsāra?
How many natures are there within the various cycles of saṃsāra?
How many distinct categories are there in the cultivation of the Buddha’s bodhi?
When returning to enter the midst of worldly toil, how many kinds of skillful means for conversion should be established to deliver all sentient beings?

I only pray that you will not forsake your great compassion for the world, enabling all practicing bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age to purify their eye of wisdom so that it shines upon the mirror of the mind, thereby fully awakening to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent!”
Excellent! Sons of good family,

it is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous meaning for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, so as to cause the bodhisattvas to purify their eyes of wisdom, and to enable all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, awaken to the true reality, and possess the patience of non-arising.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
“Good son! Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have undergone saṃsāra because of various forms of affectionate attachment and greedy desire.

Whether it be the various species in all worlds—those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, or those born by transformation—all correctly establish their life and nature through sexual desire. You should know that love is the root of saṃsāra.”
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Desire arises from craving; life exists because of desire; and sentient beings' attachment to life still relies upon the root of desire.
With desire and craving as the cause, attachment to life is the fruit.

Because various conditions of compliance and resistance arise from the realm of desire, when objects oppose the heart’s attachment, one gives rise to hatred and jealousy, thereby creating all manner of karma; for this reason, one is reborn again in the realms of hell or hungry ghosts.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, and having developed a distaste for the path of karma, one abandons evil and delights in goodness, thus manifesting again as a deva or human.

Furthermore, knowing that all attachments are to be loathed and detested, one discards attachment and delights in renunciation; yet this still nourishes the very root of craving, resulting in the manifestation of superior worldly fruits of conditioned existence. Since these are all within the cycle of saṃsāra, they do not constitute the Path of the Sages.
Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and be liberated from the cycle of saṃsāra, they must first sever greedy desire and eliminate craving. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva manifests transformations in the world, it is not rooted in desire; rather, through compassion, he causes others to relinquish their attachment, and by means of assuming various forms of greed and desire, he enters into birth and death."

If all sentient beings in the final age can renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, and diligently seek the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, they will attain awakening within their pure minds.
“Good son! All sentient beings, due to their fundamental desire, manifest the five natures with varying degrees of clarity;
these distinctions are unequal, appearing as deep or shallow based on two kinds of obstructions.”
What are the two obstacles?
First, the obstacle of principle, which obstructs right knowledge and vision; second, the obstacle of phenomena, which continues the cycle of birth and death.
What are the five natures?
"Good son! If these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is said not to have attained Buddhahood.

If sentient beings have forever abandoned sensual desire, having first eliminated the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) but not yet severed the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), they are only able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, yet are unable to manifestly abide in the realm of the Bodhisattva."
"Good son!

If all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the Great Perfectly Round Enlightenment-ocean of the Tathāgata, they should first make a vow to diligently sever the two obstacles. Once these two obstacles are subdued, they will be able to awaken to and enter the realm of the Bodhisattvas;

if the obstacles of phenomena and principle are forever severed and extinguished, they will enter the subtle and wondrous Perfectly Round Enlightenment of the Tathāgata, fulfilling both Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa."
"Good son!

All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment; when they encounter a spiritual friend and rely upon that person's practice of the Dharma for the causal stage, their cultivation will then be either sudden or gradual.

However, if they encounter the unsurpassed path of correct practice for Bodhi as taught by the Tathāgata, regardless of whether their faculties are great or small, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood."

If sentient beings, though seeking virtuous friends, encounter those with false views and have not yet attained correct awakening, this is termed the lineage of externalists; it is the fault and error of the false teacher, not the blame of the sentient beings.
This is called the differentiation of the five natures of sentient beings. "Good son!

Bodhisattvas enter all worlds solely through the skillful means of great compassion to awaken those who have not yet awakened; they even manifest various forms and appearances, as well as circumstances of both adversity and conformity, to work alongside others and transform them so that they attain Buddhahood—all of which relies upon their pure vows from time immemorial."
If all sentient beings in the final age give rise to a superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should make the pure great vows of a Bodhisattva, saying:
"May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment; in seeking spiritual friends, may I never encounter non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles."

"Relying on this vow to practice, one gradually severs all hindrances; when the hindrances are exhausted and the vow fulfilled, one ascends the pure Dharma-palace of liberation and realizes the wondrously adorned realm of Great Perfect Enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Maitreya, you should know: All sentient beings Who have not attained great liberation Do so because of their greed and desire."
Those fallen into the cycle of birth and death,
as well as those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion— without distinction in their nature—
all shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
Seeking a teacher, one attains right awakening; following the vow for bodhi, one relies upon Great Nirvana.
All Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, through their vows of great compassion, manifest entry into birth and death.
"Practitioners of the present and sentient beings of the final age who diligently sever all attachments and views shall return to Great Perfect Enlightenment. Thereupon,

the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

For our sakes, you have extensively expounded such inconceivable matters as we have never before seen or heard. Having now received the Buddha’s skillful guidance, our bodies and minds are at ease, and we have attained great benefit. We pray that for the sake of all the assembled Dharma-folk who have come here, you will again proclaim the perfect enlightened nature of the Dharma King; how do the realizations and attainments of all sentient beings, the various bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgata World-Honored Ones differ from one another?”
"May the sentient beings of the final age, upon hearing this holy teaching, follow it to achieve awakening and gradually be able to enter [the Way].
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end after each completion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good sons!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the distinctions of the gradual stages.
Listen attentively now!"
"I shall now speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
"O son of good family!

The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a nature that exists as a nature; it arises in accordance with all natures, yet is without grasping or realization. Within the true reality (dharmatā), there are in fact no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings.
Why is this? Both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations; because these illusory transformations perish, there is no one who attains realization.
It is like the faculty of the eye, which cannot see itself; their nature is inherently equal.

Regarding the absence of equality: sentient beings are deluded and inverted, unable to eliminate all illusory transformations; thus, within their false efforts regarding what is extinguished and what is not yet extinguished, they manifest distinctions.
If one attains accord with the Tathāgata’s quiescent extinction, there is in truth neither extinction nor one who extinguishes.

“Good son! Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been led by deluded notions of self and attachment to self; they have never known for themselves that [the mind] arises and perishes from moment to moment, and thus give rise to hatred and love, becoming addicted to the five desires.

If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment and clarifies the arising and ceasing [of thoughts], they will immediately know that this very life is by its own nature a laborious preoccupation.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who has forever severed weariness and anxiety and attained the purity of the Dharma-realm, yet takes that very pure understanding as a self-obstruction, they will consequently lack mastery over Perfect Enlightenment.
This is called the ordinary person’s conformity with the nature of awakening. "Good son!

All bodhisattvas take views as an obstruction; although they have severed the obstruction of views, they still dwell in the awakening to those views. Taking the obstruction of awakening as an obstruction, they lack mastery."
This is called the Bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages conforming to the nature of awakening.

"Good son! Where there is illumination and where there is awareness, both are termed obstructions. Therefore, the Bodhisattva dwells in constant awareness without abiding; illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescence. It is like a person who severs their own head: once the head is severed, there is no one left to sever."
Thus, one uses the obstructed mind to extinguish all obstructions; once obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no longer anyone who extinguishes obstructions.
The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon: if one sees the moon, one understands that what the finger points to is ultimately not the moon itself.
It is the same with the various verbal explanations and revelations given by all Tathāgatas for the sake of Bodhisattvas.
This is called the Bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.

"Good son! All obstacles are ultimate awakening; whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation; whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvāṇa; wisdom and folly are both equally prajñā; the dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are the same as bodhi; ignorance and suchness are no different realms; all precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as lust, anger, and delusion, are together the Brahma-conduct; sentient beings and lands share the same dharma-nature; hells and celestial palaces are both pure lands; those with nature and those without nature alike achieve the Buddha-way."
All afflictions are ultimately liberated; the ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm illuminates all phenomena as being like empty space.
This is called the Tathāgata’s awakening in accordance with the nature of enlightenment.

"Good son! Only those Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; who do not attempt to extinguish their deluded minds; who do not apply conscious discernment to the realm of delusive perceptions; and who, in the absence of such discernment, do not discriminate what is real—[only they can attain this]."
When those sentient beings hear this Dharma-gate, they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear.
This is what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening. Good son!
"You all should know!

Such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, as well as to great Bodhisattvas, planting the roots of all virtues;
the Buddha says that such persons are called those who have accomplished all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Pure Wisdom, you should know: The nature of perfect enlightenment Is without grasping and without realization; Therein are neither bodhisattvas nor sentient beings."
Between the time of awakening and the time before awakening, there is a gradual distinction;
sentient beings are hindered by their own understanding, while Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended conceptualization.
Upon entering the stages, they attain eternal quiescence and do not dwell in any signs.
The Great Awakening is fully perfected, And is called "Universal Accordance.
If sentient beings in the final age Do not give rise to delusions in their minds,
The Buddha says that such people Are Bodhisattvas in this very life.
"Having made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, their merit is already perfected;
though they possess many skillful means, these are all termed 'Conformity Wisdom.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

You have extensively analyzed for us such accordance with the nature of awakening, enabling all Bodhisattvas to receive the luminosity of the awakened mind through the Buddha’s perfect voice, thereby attaining wholesome benefit without depending on further cultivation.”
World-Honored One!

It is like a great city that has four gates; those who come from various directions do not enter by only one path. Likewise, all bodhisattvas’ adornment of Buddha-lands and their attainment of Bodhi are not accomplished through a single expedient means.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim for us all the expedient means and gradual stages, as well as how many types of practitioners there are in total,
so that the bodhisattvas in this assembly and those seeking the Mahāyāna in the final age may quickly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, excellent,
sons of good family!
It is well that you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

“Good son! The unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades the ten directions, giving birth to the Tathāgatas; it is of the same essence as all dharmas and is equal throughout. Regarding all practices, there is truly no duality.”

The skillful means that accord with these are immeasurable in number; they comprehensively encompass all that is returned to, yet according to the distinctions of their natures, there are three types.
"Good son! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they take a mind of pure awakening as their practice by taking stillness as their path;..."

By clarifying all thoughts, one awakens to the restless agitation of consciousness; as tranquil wisdom arises, the adventitious dust of body and mind is forever extinguished, whereby inner tranquility and lightness spontaneously emerge.
Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein, like reflections in a mirror.
This skillful means is called *śamatha*. "Good son!

If Bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they use their mind of pure awakening to realize that both the nature of the mind and the faculties and objects are all produced by illusion. They then give rise to various illusions to eliminate the illusionist, and transform these illusions to enlighten the illusory multitude."
Because they give rise to illusion, they are able to internally develop great compassion and pliancy; all Bodhisattvas initiate their practice from this point and gradually progress.

Those who contemplate illusion are not identical to the illusion itself, yet because that contemplation which is not identical to the illusion is itself illusory, they are forever free from the marks of illusion.
This is the perfected and wondrous practice of these Bodhisattvas, like a sprout growing from the soil.
This skillful means is called *samāpatti*. "Good son!

If bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they do not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness with their mind of pure awakening; they clearly understand that both body and mind are merely hindrances."

When there is no conscious perception and luminosity does not rely on any obstructions, one forever transcends the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction, as well as the enjoyment of worlds, bodies, and minds; their manifestations remain within the sensory fields.

Just as the resonance of a bell within a vessel radiates outward, affliction and nirvana do not obstruct or hinder one another. Thus, one can inwardly give rise to the light ease of quiescent extinction, wherein wondrous awakening accords with the realm of stillness—a state beyond the reach of one's own or others' body and mind, where the lives and spans of sentient beings are all but floating thoughts.
This skillful means is called dhyāna.
"Good son! These three Dharma-gates are all Perfect Enlightenment."

By drawing near to and following the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, one thereby attains Buddhahood; the various skillful means of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions—all their similarities and differences—rely entirely upon these three kinds of practice. If one attains perfect realization, one immediately achieves Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
"Good son!

Suppose there were someone who cultivates the noble path and brings to fruition the fruits of a hundred thousand million *koṭis* of *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*; this would not equal the merit of someone who hears this unimpeded Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment and practices it in accordance with it for even a single *kṣaṇa*."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Oṣadhī, you should know: The mind of the Unsurpassed Great Enlightenment Is, from the primordial limit, without dual characteristics; It accords with all skillful means."
Their number is indeed immeasurable,
yet they comprise three types: the tranquility of śamatha is like a mirror reflecting all images.
The samādhi like an illusion is like a sprout gradually growing;
dhyāna is solely quiescent extinction, like the gong within its vessel.
All these are in accord with awakening, as taught by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
"And all the great Bodhisattvas, / By means of this, have attained the Way.
/ Because these three matters are perfectly realized, / It is called ultimate Nirvana.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
Such a Dharma-gate is truly rare!
O World-Honored One!”
Regarding these various skillful means, how many modes of cultivation do all Bodhisattvas employ within the gateway of Perfect Enlightenment?
I pray that you will provide skillful instruction for the sake of this great assembly and sentient beings of the future age, so that they may awaken to the true nature of reality.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Varaprabha, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Sons of good family,
it is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation for the sake of this great assembly and for the sentient beings of the future age.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśvabhāṣin received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

“Good son! For all Tathāgatas, the perfect enlightenment of pure original awakening is fundamentally without cultivation or a cultivator. All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, however, rely on the power of illusion due to their lack of realization to practice; at that time, there are twenty-five kinds of wheels of pure meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

“If Bodhisattvas grasp only at extreme stillness, by the power of that stillness they will forever sever afflictions and achieve ultimate perfection, entering Nirvāṇa without rising from their seats.”
This Bodhisattva is one who practices śamatha alone.

If a Bodhisattva contemplates only that all things are like illusions, yet by the power of the Buddha manifests various functions within transformed worlds, fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva, and without losing silent mindfulness and various tranquil wisdoms regarding dhāraṇīs—this Bodhisattva is one who practices samāpatti alone.

"If Bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions, do not engage in active functions, and exclusively sever their afflictions, such that when the afflictions are completely severed they realize the true reality—
these Bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* alone."
"If a bodhisattva first attains ultimate stillness and, with a mind of still wisdom, illuminates all illusions, thereby initiating the practice of a bodhisattva within that state;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*."
"If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of tranquility, they then sever the afflictions and forever transcend birth and death;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first practiced śamatha and subsequently practiced dhyāna."

“If a bodhisattva, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifests various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings, and subsequently cuts off afflictions to enter nirvana;
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, then cultivated *samāpatti*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.”
"If Bodhisattvas, having severed afflictions through the power of ultimate tranquility, subsequently initiate the pure and wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva to deliver all sentient beings—
such Bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *śamatha*, then practiced *dhyāna* in the middle, and finally practiced *samāpatti* at the end."
"If a bodhisattva uses the power of ultimate stillness to sever afflictions with the mind, and further delivers sentient beings while establishing worlds—
this bodhisattva is said to have previously cultivated *śamatha* and is now practicing *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* in equal measure."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, first engenders transformations and subsequently severs afflictions,
this bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha and samāpatti simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna."
"If a bodhisattva employs the power of ultimate stillness to support quiescence, and subsequently gives rise to functional activity within transformed realms;
this bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha and dhyāna concurrently, followed by the cultivation of samāpatti."
"If a bodhisattva, through the power of transformation, adapts in various ways and thereby attains ultimate stillness,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, takes up various realms and thereby attains cessation;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated samāpatti and subsequently cultivated dhyāna."
“If there are bodhisattvas who perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abiding in tranquility while severing afflictions;
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced samāpatti, next practiced śamatha, and finally practiced dhyāna.”
"If a bodhisattva, through the unimpeded functioning of transformative power, abides in ultimate stillness by severing the afflictions,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *samāpatti*, then cultivated *dhyāna*, and finally cultivated *śamatha*."
"If a bodhisattva, through the skillful application of the power of transformation, accords with both tranquility and cessation;
such a bodhisattva is said to have previously cultivated *samāpatti* and now cultivates *śamatha* and *dhyāna* in equal measure."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, gives rise to various functions to support ultimate stillness and subsequently severs the afflictions,
this bodhisattva is said to practice samāpatti and śamatha simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, supports their state of cessation and subsequently abides in pure,
effortless meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this bodhisattva is said to practice *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of *śamatha*."
"If a bodhisattva, through the power of cessation, gives rise to ultimate stillness and abides in purity;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated śamatha."
"If bodhisattvas initiate activity through the power of quiescence, their functioning will accord with quiescence regarding all objects;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated samāpatti."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of quiescence and various intrinsic natures, abides in meditative concentration and gives rise to transformations;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated dhyāna, then cultivated śamatha in the middle, and finally cultivated samāpatti."
"If a bodhisattva, by the power of cessation, gives rise to functional activity through the unconditioned nature of self-existence, and their purified realm returns to meditative absorption;
such a bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *dhyāna*, then practiced *samāpatti*, and finally practiced *śamatha*."
"If a bodhisattva, through the power of quiescence and various purities, abides in meditative concentration and gives rise to transformations—
such a bodhisattva is said to have previously cultivated dhyāna, practicing śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure."
"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of cessation, supports ultimate stillness and yet gives rise to transformations;
this bodhisattva is said to practice dhyāna and śamatha in equal measure, and subsequently cultivate samāpatti."
"If Bodhisattvas employ the power of cessation to support their transformative manifestations, thereby giving rise to the wisdom of a most tranquil, pure, and luminous state;
such Bodhisattvas are said to practice both dhyāna and samāpatti simultaneously, and subsequently cultivate śamatha."

“If bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unite with all things, such that within all natures and characteristics there is no departure from the nature of enlightenment—
these bodhisattvas are said to be practicing the three kinds of self-nature purity in accordance with it.”
“Good son! These are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva; all bodhisattvas practice in this manner.

If any bodhisattvas or sentient beings of the final age rely upon these wheels, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), contemplate in stillness, and seek repentance with earnest supplication for twenty-one days.”
Place a marker upon each of the twenty-five wheels and, with a sincere heart, seek compassion;

then, as you grasp them with your hand according to the sequence, they shall be revealed through their binding, whereby one will immediately know whether the practice is sudden or gradual. If even a single thought of doubt or regret arises, success will not be attained.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Venerable Pratibhānakūṭa, you should know: The unimpeded and pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas Is born entirely in reliance upon meditative concentration.”
What are called śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna—
these three dharmas are cultivated both suddenly and gradually, comprising twenty-five types.
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all practitioners of the three periods of time [rely upon them].
There is none who does not rely on this Dharma to attain Bodhi;
except for those of sudden enlightenment, and those whose minds do not accord with the Dharma.
All Bodhisattvas, as well as sentient beings of the final age, [rely upon it].
"One should always hold this wheel, practicing it diligently in accordance with it;
by relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, one will before long realize nirvana.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

For our sakes, you have extensively expounded such inconceivable matters—the modes of practice on the causal ground of all Tathāgatas—causing this great assembly to attain what they have never experienced before. Beholding the realm of diligent suffering traversed by the Tamer throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, wherein all such exertions are like a single thought-moment, we Bodhisattvas are profoundly moved with joy and consolation."
World-Honored One!
If the nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure, for what reason is it defiled, causing all sentient beings to be deluded and confused, failing to enter [this state]?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively awaken us to the Dharma-nature, so that this great assembly and the sentient beings of the future age may become eyes for the time to come.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, making this request three times, beginning again and again from the end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
Sons of good family,
it is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means for the sake of this great assembly and for sentient beings of the future age.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

“Good son! Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have, through deluded conceptualization, clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. Taking these four inversions to be their actual self-substance, they consequently give rise to the two objects of aversion and affection.”

Within the body of falsehood, one further clings to falsehood; these two falsehoods rely upon each other to give rise to the path of false karma. Because false karma exists, there is the flow and turning of false perceptions; those who weary of this flow and turning falsely perceive nirvana.
Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening; it is not that awakening rejects those who seek to enter it, for there are those who seek to enter, yet they do not enter awakening.
Therefore, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought both lead to confusion and delusion. Why is this?

Because they have taken beginningless, primordial ignorance as their sovereign, all sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom; the very nature of their body and mind is entirely ignorance, just as a person cannot sever their own life-force.
Therefore, you should know this!

Those who love me I accord with; those who do not accord with me I treat with hatred and resentment. Because such feelings of hatred and attachment nourish ignorance, the continuous pursuit of the Path fails to achieve fulfillment.
“Good son! What is the mark of self?
It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings.”
Good son! It is like a person whose hundred joints are in harmony and who suddenly forgets his own body;
yet when the four limbs become slack and his regimen of nourishment goes astray, the mere application of needles or moxibustion makes him aware that he has a self.
Therefore, it is only when realization is attained that the essence of the self manifests. Good son!
Even when the mind attains the state of a Tathāgata and ultimately realizes pure nirvāṇa, all such [realizations] are still the mark of the self.
“Good son! What is the mark of a person?
It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization.”
Good son! One who awakens to the existence of a self no longer identifies with that self; yet the awakening itself is not a self, and the awakening is likewise [not a self].
Once awakened, one has transcended all who attain realization, for all such states are merely marks of the person.

Good son! If the mind perceives even the complete realization of nirvana as being "I," and if the mind retains a slight trace of such awakening while claiming to have fully exhausted the realization of principle, all such cases are termed the mark of personhood (pudgala-nimitta).
“Good son! What is the mark of sentient beings?
It refers to that which is beyond the reach of the self-realization of the minds of all sentient beings.”
"Good son!
It is like a person who speaks thus:
'I am a sentient being.'"
"Then one knows that when that person speaks of 'sentient beings,' they are neither 'I' nor 'them.
Why are they not 'I'? Because if 'I' were the sentient being, then it would not be 'I'."
Why is it not that? Because I am a sentient being, and I am not that "I. Good son!

However, all sentient beings who have attained realization and awakening do so in terms of "self" and "person"; yet that which is beyond the reach of the characteristics of self and person, while still maintaining something realized, is called the characteristic of a sentient being.
“Good son! What is the characteristic of life-span?

It refers to that which is illumined by the pure mind of all sentient beings and realized through awakening; it is that which the wisdom of all karma cannot perceive for itself, being like the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).”

Good son! If the mind perceives that all forms of awakening are but defilements—because both the awakening and the object of awakening do not depart from defilement—then it is like hot water melting ice:
there is no separate ice remaining. To know that the ice has melted, yet still maintain a self and an "awakening self," is likewise so.

“Good son! If sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks, even if they practice the Way with diligent effort for many kalpas, it will be merely called conditioned and they will ultimately fail to achieve any of the fruits of sainthood; therefore, this is called the final age of the True Dharma.”
Why is this? Because they take all forms of self to be nirvana; since there is something to be realized and something to be awakened to, it is called "accomplishment.
It is like a person who takes a thief for a son; his family’s wealth and treasures will never be truly accomplished.
Why is this? Those who possess attachment to the self also love Nirvana; they take the subduing of the root of attachment to the self as the mark of Nirvana.

Those who harbor hatred toward the self also hate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); because they do not realize that attachment to the self is the true nature of birth-and-death, they instead direct their hatred toward birth-and-death itself, which is called "not being liberated."
"How should one know that dharmas are not liberated? Good son!
Those beings of the final age who practice for Bodhi take their own slight realization to be self-purification, yet they have still not exhausted the root of the mark of self."
Furthermore, if someone praises that Dharma, they immediately feel joy and desire to deliver [others];
yet if someone slanders what has been attained therein, they immediately give rise to resentment and hatred.

Thus you should know that the mark of self is firmly grasped and maintained, lying latent within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), sporting among the various sense faculties without ever ceasing.
Good son! Because those who practice the Way do not eliminate the mark of self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
"Good son!

If one knows that the self is empty, there is no one who destroys the self; yet when I preach the Dharma, it is because my [conventional] self has not yet been severed. It is the same for sentient beings and the life-span."
“Good son! In the final age, sentient beings will mistake illness for the Dharma; therefore, they are called those who are to be pitied.
Although they apply themselves with diligent effort, they only increase their various ailments, and thus they cannot enter pure awakening.”
"Good son!
Sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks; taking the Tathāgata’s understanding and his sphere of practice as their own cultivation, they ultimately fail to achieve success."

There may be sentient beings who claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized; upon seeing those who have made superior progress, they give rise to envy.
Because such beings have not severed their attachment to self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
"Good son! If sentient beings in the final age desire to attain the Way, do not allow them to seek awakening, for this will only increase their learning and cause their views of self to grow.

Rather, they should diligently subdue their afflictions and give rise to great courage and vigor. Let that which is not yet attained be attained, and that which is not yet severed be severed. When greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, and jealousy no longer arise in response to objects, and when all attachments to self and others and all affectionate bonds are completely extinguished—of such a person, the Buddha says, they will gradually achieve success."

"Seeking a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) prevents one from falling into false views; yet, if one gives rise to hatred or attachment toward those sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Pure Action, you should know: All sentient beings..."
All arise from grasping at a self and craving;
through beginningless false wandering, if the four kinds of marks are not eliminated, one cannot achieve bodhi.
Love and hatred are born in the mind, and flattery and crookedness persist in all thoughts.
Therefore, one is greatly bewildered and distressed, unable to enter the City of Awakening.
If one can take refuge in the Land of Enlightenment, first eliminating greed, hatred, and delusion,
and ensuring that craving for dharmas does not dwell in the mind, one may gradually achieve accomplishment.
My body originally does not exist; from what cause could hatred and love arise?
This person seeks a virtuous friend and will never fall into wrong views.
If one seeks with a distracted mind, in the end nothing will be accomplished.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Pujue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
Please speak of the ailments of dhyāna!
Let the great assembly attain what they have never experienced before, so that their minds may be cleared away and they obtain great peace and stability.
World-Honored One!

In the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha; worthy sages will remain hidden while false teachings blaze ever more fiercely. Thus, what kind of person should these sentient beings seek?
Upon what kind of Dharma should they rely?
What practices should one perform?
What ailments should one eliminate?
How should one resolve the mind so that those who are blind do not fall into false views?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

Sons of good family, you are indeed able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such practice; you can bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Path, enabling those beings to attain the Holy Way.
"Listen now attentively!
I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening (Pujue) received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

“Good son! When sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve upon the Great Mind and seek out virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) with the desire to practice, they should seek those who possess correct knowledge and vision.

The mind does not dwell on signs and does not cling to the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; though manifesting amidst the afflictions of the world, the mind remains ever pure. He displays the appearance of various faults while praising the holy life (brahmacarya), ensuring that sentient beings do not fall into non-discipline.
One who seeks such a person will immediately attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
sentient beings in the final age should make offerings to such a person, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.

That spiritual friend constantly manifests purity within the four modes of conduct; even when manifesting various forms of faults and afflictions, his mind is free from arrogance, let alone regarding the accumulation of wealth, wife, children, or kinsmen.

If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that virtuous friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment; the flower of his mind will burst forth in brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
“Good son! The sublime Dharma realized by those spiritual friends should be free from the four illnesses.
What are the four illnesses?
First is the "disease of fabrication. If there is a person who speaks thus:

"I shall perform various practices within my original mind, desiring to seek perfect enlightenment," then because that nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through fabrication, it is called a disease.
Second is the illness of indolence: if there are those who say, "We shall neither sever birth-and-death nor seek nirvana;

regarding nirvana and birth-and-death, we harbor no thought of arising or ceasing; we shall leave everything as it is and follow the nature and desires of all phenomena to seek perfect enlightenment."
"Because that nature of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) does not exist by mere chance, it is called a 'sickness.
Third is the sickness of cessation:
if there is someone who says, 'I shall now cause all thoughts in my own mind to cease forever and attain the nature of all things; being tranquil and equanimous, I seek Perfect Enlightenment.'"
"Because that nature of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-gotra) is not something attained through cessation, it is called a 'sickness.
Fourth is the sickness of extinction: if there is someone who speaks thus:

'I shall now forever sever all afflictions; my body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent—how much more so the false realms of the sense organs and objects? All is eternally tranquil,' and yet seeks Perfect Enlightenment [through this]."
Because that nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a state of quiescence, it is called "sickness.
One who is free from these four sicknesses knows purity. To practice such contemplation is called right contemplation; any other contemplation is called wrong contemplation.

“Good son! Those living beings of the final age who wish to practice should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual teachers. When those spiritual teachers come to approach them, they should sever arrogance; if the teachers distance themselves, they should sever resentment.

Regarding the manifestation of favorable and adverse conditions as being like empty space, they should realize that body and mind are ultimately equal and identical in essence with all sentient beings, without distinction. Practicing in this way, one will enter Perfect Enlightenment.”
"Good son!

Sentient beings in the final age fail to achieve the Way because they have not yet attained liberation due to the seeds of self and other, and of hatred and love, which have existed since beginningless time."
If, moreover, there is a person who regards an enemy as their own parent with a mind free from duality, they will immediately eliminate all illnesses;
regarding all phenomena, the same applies to one's own and others' hatred and love.
"Good son!
Sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek Perfect Enlightenment should resolve their minds and speak these words:

'All sentient beings throughout the entirety of space, I shall cause them all to enter ultimate Perfect Enlightenment; within that Perfect Enlightenment, there shall be no one who grasps at enlightenment, having eliminated all marks of "that," "self," and "person."'"
"By generating the mind in this way, one does not fall into false views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
