"Pu-jue, you should know: In the final age, all sentient beings..."
If you seek a virtuous friend, you should seek one who possesses right view and whose mind is far removed from the two vehicles.
Within the Dharma, eliminate the four maladies: namely, effort, cessation, indifference, and extinction.
Draw near to them without pride, and distance yourself from them without anger or resentment.
When seeing various phenomena, one’s mind should give rise to a sense of wonder, as if a Buddha had appeared in the world.
Not transgressing what is not the discipline, the root of precepts is forever pure;
delivering all sentient beings, they ultimately enter Perfect Enlightenment.
Free from the marks of self, other, and person, they constantly rely upon wisdom.
"One shall immediately transcend false views and realize awakening and parinirvāṇa.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
For our sakes, you have extensively expounded upon the various skillful means of pure enlightenment, so that sentient beings of the final age may achieve great benefit.
World-Honored One!

We have now attained awakening; however, for those sentient beings of the final age who have not yet attained awakening after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should they dwell in seclusion to cultivate this pure realm of perfect enlightenment?
Within this Perfect Enlightenment, which of these three kinds of pure contemplations is the foremost?
We pray that, out of great compassion, you will bestow great benefit upon this great assembly and all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, noble sons!
That you are able to question the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means, thereby bestowing great benefit upon all sentient beings, is truly commendable.
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.

“Good son! Among all sentient beings—whether during the Buddha’s lifetime, after his parinirvāṇa, or at the end of the Dharma—there may be those who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna and, having faith in the Buddha’s secret, great, perfectly enlightened mind, wish to practice it. If they dwell within a monastery with a community of followers, they should contemplate and investigate according to their capacity as I have already explained, provided there are no other external circumstances.

If, however, they are free from such external causes and conditions, they should establish a site for the Way (a *bodhimaṇḍa*) and set a time limit: a long term of one hundred and twenty days, a medium term of one hundred days, or a short term of eighty days, and arrange a pure dwelling.”
If the Buddha is present, one should practice right reflection;

if after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one establishes an image and maintains it with mental focus and visual contemplation, giving rise to right mindfulness, this will be equivalent to the days when the Tathāgata dwells among us.
Hanging up banners and flowers for twenty-one days, one should prostrate before the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeking mercy and repenting;
upon encountering auspicious signs, the mind will attain lightness and tranquility.
After twenty-one days have passed, one should continuously maintain focused mindfulness.

If it is the beginning of summer and the three-month *varṣā* retreat, one should dwell as a pure Bodhisattva; the mind should remain detached from the *śrāvakas*, without depending on a retinue of followers.
On the day of the *varṣā* retreat, one should speak thus before the Buddha:

"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā] named so-and-so, who has mounted the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescent extinction, together enter the maintenance of the pure true reality (*dharmatā*). Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I dwell in peace within body and mind through the wisdom of the equality of nature; for the self-nature of nirvāṇa is free from all attachments."

I now respectfully request not to rely on the Śrāvakas, but rather to enter the three-month summer retreat with the Tathāgatas and Great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; for the sake of cultivating the great causal conditions for the supreme, wondrous enlightenment of a Bodhisattva, I shall not bind myself to a retinue of disciples.
"Good son! This is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat; once the three-month period has passed, he may go wherever he wishes without hindrance. Good son!"

If those sentient beings practicing in the final age who seek the Bodhisattva path and enter the three periods of cultivation do not grasp at any of the realms they have heard of, then they will ultimately never be taken by them.
“Good son! If sentient beings practice *śamatha*, they first grasp at ultimate stillness and do not give rise to thoughts; when stillness reaches its peak, they become aware.
Thus, in this initial stillness, it extends from a single body to a single world, and awareness is likewise.”
"Good son!

If one's awakening pervades a single world-system, one is able to know every single thought that arises in even a single sentient being within that world-system; it is the same for hundreds of thousands of world-systems.
Yet, none of those objects perceived by others can ever be grasped."

“Good son! If sentient beings practice samāpatti, they should first bring to mind the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, relying on various gateways to gradually practice the samādhi of diligent effort, extensively making great vows to perfume themselves and form seeds;
they must never grasp at any of the objects perceived within those realms.”

“Good son! If sentient beings practice *dhyāna*, they first take up the method of counting (*gaṇanā*). Within their minds, they clearly understand the arising, abiding, and ceasing of thoughts, as well as their limits and numerical totals. Thus, throughout the four postures, they distinguish and count thoughts until there is nothing they do not clearly know. Gradually progressing further, they eventually come to know even a single drop of rain within hundreds of thousands of worlds, as clearly as if seeing an object being used before one’s eyes;
yet, all objects of experience that are merely heard of cannot ultimately be grasped by them.”
This is called the preliminary skillful means for the three contemplations.
If sentient beings universally cultivate these three types of diligent application and vigor, it is said that a Tathāgata has appeared in the world.

If, in the final age, sentient beings of dull faculties desire to seek the Way but fail to achieve success due to karmic obstructions from the past, they should diligently repent and constantly give rise to aspiration. First, they must sever hatred, attachment, jealousy, and flattery; then, seeking a superior and exalted mind, they should study one of the three pure contemplations. Once this contemplation is undertaken, they should not practice another; with the mind never wavering or abandoning the path, they should gradually seek realization.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Perfect Enlightenment, you should know:
all sentient beings who seek the unsurpassed path should first establish a three-period commitment."
Repent of karmic deeds from beginningless time;
thereafter, engage in right reflection: that which is not within the realm of what has been heard cannot ultimately be grasped.
Rightly maintaining samādhi and the clear enumeration of dhyāna—
this is called the threefold pure contemplation.
If one can diligently practice this, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
"One should always diligently repent of all sins from beginningless time;
when all obstacles are dissolved, the realm of the Buddha will manifest before one.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
For our sakes and for the sake of sentient beings in the future age, you have extensively expounded and awakened us to such inconceivable matters.
World-Honored One!”
What are the names of this Mahāyāna teaching?
How should it be upheld?
What merit do sentient beings obtain by practicing it?
"How may I protect those who uphold this sutra?
To what extent shall I cause this teaching to spread?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end each time.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good sons!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the merits and names of such scriptural teachings."
"Listen attentively now!
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

“Good son! This sutra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers; it is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, taken as refuge by the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures. This sutra is named the *Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-cakra-vajra-dhāraṇī*; it is also named the *Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*, also named the *Secret King Samādhi*, also named the *Definitive Realm of the Tathāgata*, and also named the *Distinctions of the Self-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha*. You should uphold it.”
"Good son!
This sutra reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, can fully proclaim it.
If bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this to practice, they will gradually advance until they reach the stage of Buddhahood."
"Good son!

This sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna; sentient beings with sudden faculties attain awakening through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice the gradual path."
"Just as the great ocean does not refuse even small streams, such that even mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras who drink its water all obtain full satisfaction.
'Good son!'"

Suppose there were someone who filled the three thousandfold world-system entirely with the seven treasures and offered them as a gift; this would not equal the merit of someone who hears the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning.
"Good son!

Suppose there were someone who taught as many sentient beings as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers to attain the fruit of Arhatship; this would not equal someone who proclaims and explains even half a verse of this sutra."
"Good son!

If there is another person who, upon hearing the name of this sutra, develops faith and is free from doubt, you should know that such a person has not merely planted roots of merit and wisdom under one or two Buddhas; rather, they have planted all manner of roots of goodness under as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, having heard the teachings of this sutra."
"You, son of good family!

You should protect these practitioners in the final age, ensuring that evil Māras and various heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies and minds, causing them to fall into despondency and retreat."

At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty thousand vajras, including Agnīśikha-vajra, Praṇāśana-vajra, Nīlāmbara-vajra, and others, together with their retinues. They rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If, in the future final age, there are any sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Mahāyāna, we shall protect them as we would our own eyes;
even at the site of their practice leading to the place of enlightenment, we Vajrapāṇis, leading our own retinues, shall personally guard them morning and evening, ensuring they do not regress.
"In their households, there shall be no calamities or obstacles forever; pestilence shall be extinguished, and wealth and treasures shall abound, never lacking.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the twenty-eight celestial kings, Sumeru the King of Mountains, the Heavenly Kings who protect the nation, and others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I, too, shall protect these upholders of this sutra, constantly ensuring they remain at peace and their minds do not regress.

At that time, the great powerful ghost-king named Kumbhāṇḍa, together with one hundred thousand ghost-kings, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I, too, shall protect those who uphold this sutra, attending them morning and evening to ensure they do not falter or retreat; within a league of their dwelling, if any ghosts or spirits should invade their domain, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of spirits and their retinues, as well as the various heavenly kings, the Brahma kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Perfect Enlightenment of Complete Meaning (Mahāvaipulya-samyak-saṃbodhi-sūtra-tattvārtha)
